By manipulating memory buses, compromised systems can generate covert radio frequency signals encoding files, cryptographic keys, and biometric information. Using off-the-shelf software-defined radio hardware and simple antennas, attackers can intercept these raw emissions from a distance and translate them back into binary data.

The technique achieves a data leakage rate of up to 1,000 bits per second, presenting significant risks for high-security environments relying on network isolation. While the method requires nearby radio equipment and custom malware implementation, it highlights hardware emission vulnerabilities that bypass traditional air-gap protections. The paper also outlines potential countermeasures to detect and mitigate out-of-band memory bus emissions.

entry.title: Pivot Database Engine Explains Impact of Memory Latency on Database Performance
entry.content:
Links: pivotlake.io | hacker news

High database CPU utilization frequently masks underlying memory stalls rather than intense computation, as modern RAM access speeds lag hundreds of instructions behind CPU processing capabilities. A naive GROUP BY implementation causes frequent cache misses that force the processor to wait on cold memory from DRAM.

To mitigate this bottleneck, the Pivot database engine implements a two-phase radix partitioning approach that breaks down large aggregation tasks into smaller pieces. By ensuring that working hash tables fit within the CPU caches, this optimization significantly reduces DRAM load operations and accelerates query execution times.

entry.title: Go 1.28 HTTP/2 Parking Mechanism Reduces Server Memory Usage
entry.content:
Links: abdolirad.me | lobsters | hacker news

An analysis of the draft Go 1.28 release notes examines a new HTTP/2 server mechanism called parking, which allows connection-serving goroutines to exit when there is no active work instead of waiting idle. Benchmarks comparing a Go 1.28 development build with parking enabled versus disabled show that handling 5,000 idle HTTP/2 connections results in 5,000 fewer active goroutines and a resident set size (RSS) reduction of roughly 85 to 93 MiB.

The benchmark results indicate that enabling parking lowers stack memory usage by approximately 78 MiB under the same load, while heap allocation metrics remain variable across test runs. Because the feature is evaluated on a pre-release development build using an experimental and temporary debug setting, the findings highlight potential memory efficiency gains for servers maintaining thousands of idle connections rather than guaranteed outcomes for all workloads.

entry.title: Go Security Team Advises on Mitigating CVE-2026-98432 Linux Kernel Flaw
entry.content:
Links: groups.google.com | lobsters | hacker news

The Go Security Team has issued guidance regarding CVE-2026-98432, a critical use-after-free vulnerability affecting IPv4 TCP connection handling in the Linux kernel that can allow remote code execution when Multipath TCP listeners are exposed. While upgrading to a patched kernel remains the definitive fix, Go 1.24 and later versions enable Multipath TCP by default for listen sockets on Linux, making programs potentially susceptible unless mitigated.

Developers can disable Multipath TCP globally at runtime using the "GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0" environment variable, at build time by adding "godebug multipathtcp=0" to a go.mod file, or explicitly per socket using Dialer and ListenConfig settings. However, the security team cautions that program-by-program mitigations are fragile and stresses that updating the kernel is the only complete remedy, noting that any future changes to Go's default behavior will be discussed publicly.
